***

**(CNN) —** After nearly 150 years of continuous publication, Denver, Colorado's *Rocky Mountain News* printed its final edition on Friday, falling victim to a depressed economy and the shift toward the digital age. 

The paper’s farewell issue featured a simple front-page headline: "Goodbye, Colorado," accompanied by a poignant message to its readers: "It is with great sadness that we say goodbye to you today. Our time chronicling the life of Denver and Colorado, the nation and the world, is over."

The newspaper's parent company, the E.W. Scripps Co., delivered the news to staff at noon on Thursday, bringing an end to three months of intense speculation and anxiety following the outlet being put up for sale in December. 

The *Rocky Mountain News* stands as the latest casualty in an era marked by widespread shutdowns, layoffs, and retrenchment across the newspaper industry. "It's in a free fall and nobody knows where the bottom is. It's kind of like water in the toilet swirling around and nobody knows what's left when you're done flushing," noted media critic Eric Alterman. A video report examines how economic pressures and the rise of the Internet continue to take a severe toll on the industry.

Across the country, newspapers face mounting strain as readership and print advertising revenues plummet while a growing majority of Americans seek information online. "All newspapers are under great pressure. They'll survive, but they'll survive in different forms; their cost base will have to be dramatically lowered," said Mort Zuckerman, publisher of the *New York Daily News*, the nation's seventh-largest paper by circulation.

The sharp decline in advertising dollars during a grueling recession has forced publications to reduce costs by laying off cartoonists, columnists, and editorial staff, leaving many to search for work in a contracting sector. Pia Catton lost her position as arts editor of the *New York Sun* five months ago when the publication closed. While she currently holds a temporary assignment editing a book, she anticipates needing to explore alternative career paths soon. "There will always be a market for news; you will always need to know immediately what's happening. Will there be a market for newspapers? That's another question," she observed.

According to the *Columbia Journalism Review*, the *Rocky Mountain News* employed more than 200 editorial personnel. Rich Boehne, chief executive officer of Scripps, informed staff that the decision stemmed from severe macroeconomic headwinds, systemic industry disruption, and multimillion-dollar annual operating losses. 

"Denver can't support two newspapers any longer," Boehne stated. "It's certainly not good news for you, and it's certainly not good news for Denver."

Since 2001, the *News* had maintained a joint operating agreement with *The Denver Post*, combining commercial operations to reduce expenses while keeping their respective newsrooms independent. The closure leaves Denver served by a single major daily newspaper—a dynamic now characteristic of most American cities.

"We've been, sort of, hanging on the edge for so long," said Mel Pompanio, a presentation editor for the paper. "What a huge loss for Colorado today."

The industry's instability extends nationwide. This week, the *San Francisco Chronicle* warned that it faces potential sale or closure if it cannot stem escalating financial losses. Executives at Hearst Corp., the paper's parent company, disclosed that the publication lost $50 million in 2008 and remains on track to lose even more this year.

"It's difficult. It's hard," reflected Lynn Bartels, a political reporter and 26-year veteran at Scripps. "I haven't returned any phone calls yet, because I don't need to be reporting and crying at the same time. I've done that enough."

Video footage published on the paper's website showed a newsroom filled with solemn expressions, punctuated by quiet weeping as the reality of the closure settled in among staff. 

"I could say stupid things like 'I know how you feel.' I don't," Boehne told the gathered newsroom. "We are just deeply sorry. I hope you will accept that."

*CNN's Richard Roth contributed to this report.*

After nearly 150 years of continuous publication, the *Rocky Mountain News* printed its final edition after its parent company failed to secure a buyer. The steep decline of traditional print media is driven by a convergence of economic and technological shifts. At the root of the problem lies a combination of steadily shrinking print readerships and a dramatic drop in advertising revenues—historically the primary source of funding for newsrooms. This rapid transition shattered the long-standing economic model that sustained legacy newspapers for generations.

**Headline:** The Twilight of the Daily Print: How an Industry Crisis Reshaped American Journalism

For more than a century, the morning newspaper was an indispensable staple of daily American life. It served as the primary watchdog of local government, the record of community history, and the chief source of news and entertainment. Today, however, that legacy is under severe siege. Driven by a volatile economy and a seismic shift in consumer behavior toward digital news, traditional newspapers are facing a fight for their very survival. To endure a devastating collapse in advertising revenue, media companies have been forced into a brutal cycle of layoffs, budget cuts, and closures, signaling a dramatic transformation in how news is produced and consumed.

The roots of this crisis lie in a double-edged challenge: changing audience habits and the collapse of the traditional print business model. As internet access expanded and smartphones became ubiquitous, readers increasingly sought real-time, on-demand news, often expecting it for free. At the same time, the broader economic downturns of the early 21st century hit corporate budgets hard, causing businesses to slash their marketing spend. 

Crucially, the loss of print readers triggered a catastrophe for newspaper balance sheets. For decades, print journalism was subsidized by high-margin print advertising and lucrative classified listings. When platforms like Craigslist disrupted classifieds, and tech giants like Google and Meta captured the lion's share of digital advertising, print outlets lost their financial engine. Attempts to replace print ad revenue with digital ad revenue quickly proved ineffective, yielding only "digital pennies for print dollars."

In a desperate bid to remain solvent, newspaper executives turned to aggressive austerity. Newsrooms across the country endured wave after wave of layoffs, gutting the ranks of experienced investigative reporters, editors, and photographers. Print schedules were scaled back, delivery zones were reduced, and paper sizes shrank. Far from saving the industry, these severe cost-cutting measures often pushed papers into a quality death spiral: smaller, less comprehensive news products led to declining subscriber numbers, which in turn caused advertising revenue to plummet further.

Perhaps no single event better illustrated the grim reality of this shift than the sudden death of the *Rocky Mountain News*. Founded in 1859, the Denver-based publication was a respected, Pulitzer Prize-winning institution that had reported on the American West for nearly 150 years. Yet, despite its rich history and deep community roots, the paper succumbed to crippling financial losses. On February 27, 2009, the *Rocky Mountain News* published its final edition, bidding a heartbreaking farewell to its readers and leaving Denver as a single-newspaper town. Its closure sent shockwaves through the industry, serving as a stark warning that no legacy brand was safe.

The demise of the *Rocky Mountain News* underscored an unforgiving truth: historic print outlets cannot rely on nostalgia or past prestige to survive in the modern era. To avoid extinction, news organizations have been forced to fundamentally overhaul their operational strategies. For many, this has meant prioritizing digital-first publishing, implementing strict online paywalls, shifting toward reader-supported subscription models, or transitioning to non-profit status. 

While print media may never return to its golden era, the crisis has sparked vital innovations in digital journalism. Nevertheless, as local newspapers continue to shrink or disappear altogether, the core challenge remains. The death of print is not merely a story of failing businesses; it is a profound transformation of the public sphere, proving that while the mediums for news will inevitably evolve, the financial model supporting vital journalism must be reinvented if democracy's key watchdog is to survive.

**End of an era: Rocky Mountain News publishes final edition after 150 years**

**By CNN Staff**
**DENVER (CNN) —** For 150 years, the *Rocky Mountain News* captured the history of Colorado, reporting on everything from the West's gold rush era to modern presidential campaigns. On Friday, the newspaper wrote its own final chapter. 

With a poignant cover featuring a black-and-white photograph of a young reader from decades past and the simple headline "Goodbye, Colorado," the state’s oldest daily newspaper published its last edition. 

The closure leaves Denver as a one-newspaper town and marks one of the most high-profile casualties in an industry currently being battered by a severe recession, declining readership, and the rise of digital media.

Inside the newsroom on Thursday afternoon, the atmosphere was a mix of grief, pride, and disbelief as journalists worked on the very pages that would chronicle their own unemployment. When Editor and Publisher John Temple broke the news to the staff that parent company E.W. Scripps Co. was shutting the paper down after failing to find a buyer, the room fell silent, followed by a tearful standing ovation for the publication’s long legacy.

"It is with profound sadness that I share with you that tomorrow will be the final edition of the *Rocky Mountain News*," Temple wrote in a final, heartbreaking column to readers. "We will be saying goodbye to you, and to each other."

### A pioneer spirit silenced

Founded in 1859 by William N. Byers—nearly two decades before Colorado even achieved statehood—the *Rocky* was born in a makeshift office above a saloon, printed on a press hauled across the plains by ox cart. 

Over the next century and a half, it evolved into a journalistic powerhouse, winning four Pulitzer Prizes since 2000 alone. Known for its tabloid format, vibrant photography, and aggressive local reporting, the paper was deeply embedded in the identity of the American West.

For decades, the *Rocky* was locked in one of the nation's fiercest newspaper wars with its cross-town rival, *The Denver Post*. In 2001, in an effort to survive, the two papers entered into a Joint Operating Agreement (JOA), combining business and printing operations while keeping their newsrooms entirely separate and competitive. 

However, the arrangement could not insulate the *Rocky* from the catastrophic shifts in the media industry. E.W. Scripps reported that the paper lost $16 million in 2008. The company put the paper up for sale in December, but announced Thursday that no viable buyers had stepped forward.

"We couldn't find a buyer, and we couldn't continue to sustain the losses," Rich Boehne, chief executive officer of Scripps, said in a statement. "The economic model that sustained local newspapers for generations is broken."

### A harbinger for American journalism

The death of the *Rocky Mountain News* sent shockwaves through the journalism community, serving as a grim milestone in an industry already in freefall. Just short of its 150th anniversary, the paper became the first major metropolitan daily to close completely during the late-2000s economic downturn.

Industry analysts warn it will not be the last. Across the country, major media companies are facing bankruptcy, severe layoffs, and the threat of closure. In Seattle, the 146-year-old *Seattle Post-Intelligencer* is widely expected to shut down its print edition in the coming weeks.

"When a paper that has served a community for 150 years—and won Pulitzers just months ago—can disappear overnight, every newsroom in America feels the chill," said Laura Frank, a veteran investigative reporter for the *Rocky*.

### A final farewell

In its 52-page final issue, the newsroom delivered a compelling, highly personal farewell to its roughly 225,000 daily subscribers. The edition was packed with archival photos, historic front pages, and reflections from the staff.

Nearly 200 journalists lost their jobs on Friday, but many spent their final hours together raising a glass at a local pub across the street from the downtown office building they had occupied for decades.

As the heavy printing presses at the paper's Denver plant ground to a halt early Friday morning, printing the final copy of the iconic tabloid, a century and a half of history rolled off the line for the last time. 

The paper's final editorial closed with a message to the readers who had opened their doors to the *Rocky* since the days of the Wild West:

"We leave you today with a grateful heart," the editorial read. "Thank you for letting us into your homes and your lives for 150 years. It was our honor."

***

**DENVER, Colorado (CNN)** — The giant printing presses in the basement of 400 W. Colfax Avenue fell silent early Friday morning, bringing a grim and historic end to a pioneer of the American West. 

After nearly 150 years of continuous publication, the *Rocky Mountain News* printed its final edition today. The tabloid, born in 1859 during the Colorado Gold Rush, became the latest and most high-profile victim of a devastating economic storm that is crippling the American newspaper industry.

In a tearful newsroom gathering on Thursday afternoon, Editor and Publisher John Temple broke the news to a staff of more than 200 journalists.

### A Financial Cliff

The demise of the "Rocky" came with head-spinning speed. Its parent company, the Cincinnati-based E.W. Scripps Co., put the paper up for sale in December after it lost $16 million in 2008. Scripps warned that if a buyer could not be found, the paper would close. 

Despite Denver's status as one of the few remaining two-paper towns—where the *Rocky* engaged in a fierce, decades-long rivalry with MediaNews Group’s *The Denver Post*—no viable suitors stepped forward. A Joint Operating Agreement (JOA) signed in 2001, designed to allow both papers to share business operations while maintaining separate newsrooms, ultimately failed to shield the publication from an unprecedented drop in advertising revenue.

"The math was simple," Rich Boehne, chief executive of Scripps, said in a statement. "The Rocky was no longer profitable, and in this economic climate, we could no longer subsidize its losses."

### A Perfect Storm: Internet Disruption Meets Economic Slump

While the loss of the *Rocky* is a local tragedy for Denver, media analysts say it is a terrifying harbinger of what lies ahead for the rest of the country. 

The newspaper industry is currently caught in the crosshairs of a structural shift to digital media and the severe cyclical downturn of the Great Recession. 

For decades, daily newspapers relied on a lucrative business model: cheap subscriptions subsidized by high-margin classified ads (automotive, real estate, and employment) and display advertising from major department stores. Today, both revenue streams have evaporated.

Free online platforms like Craigslist have systematically dismantled the classified ad market, wiping out billions of dollars in revenue that sustained local newsrooms for generations. At the same time, readers are increasingly getting their news for free online through web portals, blogs, and news aggregators like Google News. 

Exacerbating these long-term digital shifts is the current global economic crisis. With the housing market in freefall, auto manufacturers on the verge of collapse, and retail sales plummeting, print advertising dollars have plummeted at double-digit rates over the past year. 

"What we are seeing is not just a standard recession slump; it is an acceleration of a permanent shift," said Ken Doctor, a media analyst with Outsell Inc. "The internet broke the monopoly that newspapers had on local information and advertising. The recession is just finishing the job."

### An Industry in Freefall

The closure of the *Rocky Mountain News* is not an isolated event. Across the nation, news organizations are desperately cutting costs, laying off reporters, and reducing print distribution days:

*   **The Tribune Company**, owner of *The Chicago Tribune*, *The Los Angeles Times*, and *The Baltimore Sun*, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in December.
*   **The Seattle Post-Intelligencer** is currently on the market and is widely expected to cease print publication in the coming weeks, potentially moving to a web-only format.
*   **The Minneapolis Star Tribune** filed for bankruptcy in January, while major chains like Gannett and McClatchy have announced thousands of layoffs industry-wide.

Even venerable institutions like *The New York Times* have been forced to take drastic measures, recently mortgaging their Manhattan headquarters and accepting a $250 million cash injection from Mexican billionaire Carlos Slim to shore up liquidity.

### The Cost to Democracy

As newspapers shutter or shrink, media watchdogs are raising alarms about the impact on civic life. A smaller press corps means fewer reporters covering city halls, state capitals, courtrooms, and school boards.

With the *Rocky* shuttered, *The Denver Post* becomes the sole daily newspaper in a metropolitan area of 2.8 million people.

"When a newspaper dies, a community loses its mirror," said Alex Jones, director of the Shorenstein Center on the Press, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard University. "Bloggers and aggregators don't do investigative reporting. They don't sit through eight-hour city council meetings. If we lose local daily journalism, who is going to hold local power brokers accountable?"

Back in Denver, the journalists of the *Rocky Mountain News* packed up their desks on Friday morning, joining the ranks of thousands of unemployed media workers navigating an uncertain future. 

For a century and a half, the paper was tossed onto Denver doorsteps every morning, chronicling the rise of a boomtown. Today, Denver woke up to a quieter morning, and an industry looks toward an increasingly uncertain digital horizon.

Scripps, the paper’s parent company, had failed to find a buyer. After 149 years, 55 days short of its 150th anniversary, the *Rocky Mountain News* was closing its doors. Effective immediately.

The next day’s paper—Friday, February 27, 2009—would be its last.

The shuttering of the *Rocky* was a watershed moment in American media. It was not just the story of one city losing a beloved tabloid; it was the clearest signal yet that the century-old financial model sustaining daily American print journalism was collapsing under the weight of the digital age and the Great Recession.

### Tears and Typewriters: The Final Hours in the Newsroom

When John Temple delivered the news, weeping staff members embraced one another. Some stared at their screens in stunned silence; others reached for their phones to call loved ones.

"To Denver and Colorado, we say goodbye," Temple told the gathered journalists, his voice cracking with emotion. "It is with deep sadness that I tell you that tomorrow will be the final edition of the *Rocky Mountain News*."

Despite the crushing grief, the newsroom went to work. In a display of gallows humor and fierce professional pride, the journalists spent their final hours covering the death of their own paper. Photographers who had won Pulitzer Prizes for the publication turned their lenses on their weeping colleagues. Reporters wrote eulogies for a masthead that had reported on Colorado since before it was even a state, having been founded in 1859 during the Pikes Peak Gold Rush.

The final edition featured a simple, poignant front cover: a black-and-white photograph of staff members comforting one another, overlaid with the words: *"FINAL EDITION: Goodbye, Colorado."* Inside was a 52-page special section chronicling the paper’s history, from its origin as a pioneer sheet printed on a hand press to its modern era as a digital-age tabloid known for its sharp writing and striking visual photojournalism.

"We knew the industry was in trouble, but no one believed a paper this good, with this much history, could just vanish overnight," recalled one veteran editor. "It felt like a death in the family, except the family was also out of a job."

### The Economic Avalanche

The *Rocky* had been locked in a fierce, decades-long newspaper war with its cross-town rival, the *Denver Post*. For years, Denver was one of the few remaining two-newspaper towns in America, celebrated for the fierce competition that drove both outlets to produce high-caliber journalism. 

In 2001, the two papers entered into a Joint Operating Agreement (JOA), combining their business, advertising, and printing operations through the Denver Newspaper Agency while keeping their newsrooms entirely separate and competitive. 

It was meant to save both papers. Instead, it merely delayed the inevitable. 

By 2008, the severe economic downturn compounded a deeper structural shift. Print advertising revenues—long the lifeblood of daily newspapers—were plummeting. Classified advertising, which once accounted for up to 40% of newspaper revenue, was largely swallowed up by free online alternatives like Craigslist. Readers were moving online, where news was expected to be free, and digital advertising yielded only pennies on the dollar compared to traditional print ads.

In 2008 alone, the *Rocky Mountain News* lost $16 million. When Scripps put the paper up for sale in December of that year, only one potential buyer made an offer, but failed to show the financial capability to complete the purchase.

### Media Experts: A Systemic Collapse

The demise of the *Rocky Mountain News* sent shockwaves through the journalism world, prompting media analysts to declare that the traditional business model for print newspapers was fundamentally broken.

"What happened in Denver was the canary in the coal mine," said Rick Edmonds, a media business analyst at the Poynter Institute. "It wasn't that people stopped reading the *Rocky Mountain News*—it actually had strong readership. The fundamental problem was that the economic engine driving print journalism crashed. Advertising dollars disappeared faster than anyone predicted, and digital revenue couldn't fill the chasm."

Media analyst Alan Mutter, author of the *Reflections of a Newsosaur* blog, argued that the industry’s slow response to technology was its undoing. "Newspapers made a catastrophic error early in the internet era by giving away their content for free online," Mutter noted at the time. "They taught a generation of readers that high-quality journalism had no monetary value, while simultaneously failing to build a modern ad-tech infrastructure. When print revenues fell off a cliff in 2008, papers like the *Rocky* had no safety net."

Experts also pointed out the democratic cost of losing legacy institutions. 

"When a paper like the *Rocky* closes, you don't just lose jobs; you lose civic oversight," said Ken Doctor, a news industry analyst and author. "You go from two newsrooms competing to uncover corruption and hold local government accountable to one diminished newsroom. A one-newspaper town—or worse, a news desert—is a loss for the entire community."

### A Harbinger of the Future

The closure of the *Rocky Mountain News* was not an isolated event; it was the beginning of a grim trend. Just weeks later, the *Seattle Post-Intelligencer* ceased print publication to become an online-only outlet. Months after that, the *Tucson Citizen* and the *Ann Arbor News* shuttered. Major publishing houses across the country slipped into bankruptcy.

In the years following the *Rocky's* death, Denver was left solely to the *Denver Post*, which itself would later suffer massive hedge-fund cost-cutting, leading to a drastically reduced newsroom. 

On February 27, 2009, as the final delivery trucks rolled out of the printing plant in the pre-dawn darkness carrying the last copies of the *Rocky Mountain News*, an era in American media quietly ended. The paper left behind a legacy of Pulitzer Prizes, generations of loyal readers, and a sobering lesson: in the digital age, even the most cherished traditions offer no immunity against economic evolution.

**THE DAY THE PRESSES STOPPED: How the early digital rush dismantled local journalism**

**DENVER —** On the morning of February 27, 2009, readers across Colorado picked up a piece of history that doubled as an obituary. The front page of the *Rocky Mountain News* featured a nostalgic black-and-white photograph of its early days, accompanied by two simple words: “Final Edition.” 

Just two months shy of its 150th anniversary, Colorado’s oldest newspaper printed its last issue, laying off more than 200 journalists and leaving a major American city with only one daily paper. 

While the closure was a local tragedy for Denver, it served as a national bellwether. The demise of the *Rocky* became the most dramatic symbol of a catastrophic era for American print journalism, as the rapid rise of the internet dismantled a business model that had sustained local news for over a century.

### The Digital Disruption

For decades, local newspapers operated as lucrative geographic monopolies or duopolies. They were funded by a high-margin business model built on three pillars: print subscriptions, display advertising from local retailers, and classified advertising. 

By the mid-2000s, the internet systematically dismantled all three.

The first and most fatal blow came to the classifieds section—historically known as the "cash cow" of local print news. Web platforms like Craigslist offered free, searchable listings for jobs, housing, and used cars. Virtually overnight, billions of dollars in classified revenue evaporated from newspaper balance sheets nationwide. 

At the same time, news consumers were migrating online, expecting content to be free. Newspapers, eager to capture web traffic, initially gave away their reporting on basic, unmonetized websites. But advertising online proved vastly different from print. Print advertisers paid top dollar for guaranteed eyes on a physical page; online advertisers bought targeted clicks for fractions of a cent. Publishers realized too late that they had traded "analog dollars for digital pennies."

### The Battle for Denver

In Denver, the digital transition was exacerbated by a legendary, cutthroat newspaper war. For decades, the tabloid-style *Rocky Mountain News* (owned by E.W. Scripps Co.) had fought fiercely against the broadsheet *The Denver Post* (owned by MediaNews Group). 

In 2001, in an attempt to survive rising costs, the two papers entered a Joint Operating Agreement (JOA). They merged their business, printing, and advertising operations while keeping their newsrooms separate and aggressively competitive.

However, the JOA was built for a print-dominated world. As online reading habits accelerated between 2005 and 2008, print circulation for both papers plummeted. The *Rocky*, despite winning four Pulitzer Prizes in its final decade, was losing millions of dollars a year.

In late 2008, as the global financial crisis compounded the internet’s disruptive force, Scripps put the *Rocky* up for sale. With the real estate market collapsing and digital migration in full swing, no viable buyers emerged. 

"We no longer see a way to make the *Rocky* profitable," Scripps CEO Rich Boehne announced when the closure was finalized. 

### A Domino Effect Across America

The death of the *Rocky Mountain News* was not an isolated event; it was the opening crest of a tidal wave that swept through the news industry in the late 2000s.

Just three weeks after the *Rocky* closed, the 146-year-old *Seattle Post-Intelligencer* printed its final edition, transitioning to a scaled-back, web-only newsroom before eventually fading away. Around the same time, the Tribune Company—owner of *The Chicago Tribune*, the *Los Angeles Times*, and *The Baltimore Sun*—slid into bankruptcy. Across the country, newsrooms slashed staff, shuttered statehouse bureaus, and cut back on investigative units.

According to data from the Pew Research Center, U.S. newspaper ad revenue fell from a peak of nearly $50 billion in 2005 to under $25 billion by 2011—a unprecedented collapse in modern media history. 

### The Lasting Legacy

In the newsroom of the *Rocky* on its final night, weeping reporters and editors scrambled to finish stories they knew would be their last. Editor John Temple famously chronicled the paper's final days in a poignant, self-reflective photo essay published in the farewell edition.

The loss of the *Rocky* left Denver as a "one-paper town," a reality that civic leaders at the time warned would diminish local accountability. In the years that followed, the remaining *Denver Post* would itself endure severe hedge-fund cuts, leaving the city with a fraction of the journalists it had in the 1990s.

The late 2000s marked the end of print journalism’s golden era and forced the industry into a painful, ongoing evolution toward digital subscriptions, non-profit newsrooms, and newsletter models. But for media historians, the silent presses in Denver on February 27, 2009, remain the definitive moment the digital age truly caught up to the printed word.
